rv.q: The reimagined "Side Show" that opened Monday night at the St. James Theatre is a stunning, soaring, must-see musical.

This beautiful and wrenching musical, lovingly directed by Bill Condon, asks us to step inside their skins and feel what it’s like to be celebrated one moment, rejected the next, and to have the strange consolation of a companion who shares it all: the pain, the joy, the hope, the frustration.

Condon created a big, old-fashioned, shamelessly entertaining musical that tells its human story while embracing, without forcing, issues beyond the showbiz saga of the sisters' sensational and sad freak show/vaudeville/Hollywood lives.

Bill Condon's fabulous 'revisal' maximizes the material's strengths and minimizes its weaknesses, serving up mesmerizing entertainment veined throughout with haunting poignancy...Condon puts the sideshow exhibits on lurid display, starting with the intoxicating opening number, 'Come Look at the Freaks.'
Both actresses are impeccable, funny and affecting.
It's a pleasure to report that this tiptop production has realized much of the potential of this show

Leading ladies Emily Padgett and Erin Davie are perfection as Daisy and Violet Hilton, conjoined twins in real life who were plucked out of a carnival midway by a rascal showman and transformed into vaudeville stars.
The problem with Side Show is that these stories can’t be separated, and only one can thrive.

The revival of 'Side Show' is a sumptuous production that showcases the considerable talents of Erin Davie and Emily Padgett as conjoined twins Daisy and Violet Hilton, but the musical itself remains a problematic work.
Instead, this show looks too often toward its own ending.
But while this sincere and stylishly designed production is perhaps the best that Side Show can be, that best, alas, isn’t great.
"Side Show" now takes its place in the pantheon of great American musicals.
The show's heart remains in the right place, and its leads are superb. But the material still feels more earnest than inspired.
Condon's production is a stunning achievement and a must-see attraction for anyone who cares about serious, Sondheim-style musical theater.
Still, there’s something amiss in this new “Side Show.”

For a musical about true-life conjoined twins Daisy and Violet Hilton, the strange and stirring 'Side Show' has a nagging habit of losing its grip. Chalk it up to dramatic inconsistencies and thin characterizations.
Certainly not this leaden, sporadically moving update—which bears little resemblance to the original production.
Still, there is a great deal of talent prancing around on that stage, and you could do worse than share an evening enjoying them all.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this revised cult musical about the Hilton conjoined twins, praising the powerful performances and emotional score but citing persistent story and character problems that revisions couldn't fully fix.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at St. James Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well.
At 1,710 seats, St. James Theatre is one of the larger Broadway houses — far side mezzanine seats sit well off-axis and a long way from the stage.

vs.sum: The St. James Theatre offers good sightlines for most seats, though the lack of a solid rake can be an issue if someone tall sits in front of you. The sound quality is generally good, but the tight legroom can be uncomfortable for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic and grand interior, while facilities are average with standard amenities.

acc.note: No steps from sidewalk to Orchestra. No elevator. Mezzanine up 29 steps, Balcony up 76 steps.
